tasks.short: Run the emergency checklist, declare the emergency and coordinate with air traffic control and the cabin, decide on diversion, log the defect, hand it to maintenance, write the air safety report and submit it.

steps.what: Airline pilot responds to in-flight emergencies and malfunctions with the checklist
Airline pilot declares the emergency and coordinates with air traffic control and the cabin
Airline pilot decides on diversion with dispatch
Airline pilot writes the defect in the technical log and signs it: on paper today; in the electronic log after the change, with aircraft and flight filled in
Airline pilot checks the final defect entry: the defect described matches what happened, and aircraft and defect type are right
Airline pilot releases the signed defect entry to maintenance: hands over the paper page on arrival today; after the change sends it from the tablet
Airline pilot writes the air safety report on the in-flight emergency: on a paper form today; after the change in a form with flight, times and position filled in
Airline pilot checks the final air safety report: the narrative matches what happened, and the filled-in flight, times and position are right
Airline pilot submits the checked air safety report to the safety department: by e-mail today; from the form after the change

tasks.design: Defects go into an electronic technical log on the flight-deck tablet ({OPS_SYSTEM}) with aircraft and flight filled in; the pilot writes the defect, checks the entry and signs, and the signed entry syncs to maintenance, so they prepare before the aircraft lands. The air safety report form fills flight, times and position from the operations data; the pilot writes the narrative, checks the report and submits it to the safety department. Handling the emergency, talking with air traffic control and deciding on diversion stay with the crew.
tasks.previous_blocker: Defects were handwritten in a paper log and reports filled in after landing.
tasks.enabler_now: Electronic technical logs sync to maintenance; report forms prefill from flight data.
tasks.still_hard: After an emergency crews are tired and reports still take care.
tasks.human_edge: Choosing the safest airport when two systems fail at once.

evidence.claim: Three months after an electronic technical log went live on 140+ aircraft, calls to maintenance control fell by more than 25%.
Aviation products sit in AI Act Annex I, so AI rules come through EASA; this design uses no AI.

assumptions: Boundary: from the malfunction to the submitted report; the investigation is outside.
Input contract: flight data from the operations system; defect types set by maintenance; fallback is paper log and form.

Emergency handling and decisions keep their full time, and so do both checks. s4 keeps 80 because only aircraft and flight fill in and the pilot writes the defect; s6 keeps 75 because only flight, times and position fill in and the pilot writes the narrative; s5 keeps 30 for the send and s7 keeps 20 for submitting the form.
The authority approves the electronic log before use.
research_questions: Do defects get fixed on the next turnaround more often?

incremental.description: Airline pilot syncs the tablet if it was offline.

approvals.approved_version: The defect entry with aircraft, defect description and signature exactly as checked by the pilot in s4c, synced once to maintenance for this aircraft; any change needs a new check and signature.
The air safety report with narrative, flight, times and position exactly as checked by the pilot in s6c, submitted once to the safety department; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: the electronic log is approved for only part of the fleet, so about half of defects stay on paper pages handed over on arrival (s4 keeps 90, s5 keeps 65) (8.2); high: the whole fleet uses the electronic log (10.1).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Contact the tower for clearances and instructions by radio, read back and note clearances, listen to the airport weather broadcast, and follow the instructions.

steps.what: Airline pilot contacts control towers for takeoff clearances and arrival instructions using radio equipment
Airline pilot takes the departure clearance: by voice with read-back and writing it down today; after the change, where the airport offers datalink, reads it on the display
Airline pilot checks the datalink clearance against the flight plan: route, runway, altitude and transponder code
Airline pilot accepts the checked clearance by datalink
Airline pilot listens to the airport weather and runway broadcast
Airline pilot follows and confirms the instructions

tasks.design: Where the airport offers it, the departure clearance and the airport weather broadcast arrive by datalink on the flight-deck display ({OPS_SYSTEM}), so pilots read rather than copy them by hand and listen to the broadcast less often. Radio contact with the tower and following instructions stay with the pilots.
tasks.previous_blocker: Clearances and airport information came only by voice and were written down.
tasks.enabler_now: Many airports offer datalink departure clearances and weather broadcasts.
tasks.still_hard: Busy airports and changes on the ground still need voice.
tasks.human_edge: Catching a clearance meant for a similar call sign.

evidence.claim: Many airports deliver departure clearances and weather broadcasts by datalink to the flight deck.

assumptions: Boundary: from the flight phase to instructions followed; flight planning is outside.
Input contract: datalink services at the airport; fallback is voice.

Radio contact and following instructions keep their full time, and so do the check and acceptance of datalink clearances. About half of departures are from airports with datalink clearance and weather; s2 keeps 60 and s3 keeps 70.
The aircraft has a datalink unit.
unknowns: Share of airports with datalink clearance.

incremental.description: Airline pilot falls back to voice when a datalink clearance is rejected or times out.

approvals.approved_version: The departure clearance exactly as checked by the pilot in s2c against the flight plan, accepted once by datalink to the issuing tower; a changed clearance needs a new check and acceptance.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: few airports on the network offer datalink, so s2 and s3 keep 85 (3.9); high: about half of departures use datalink as assumed (9.4).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Monitor engine and system displays, check fuel against the flight plan at waypoints, note fuel and times, and discuss abnormal trends with the other pilot.

steps.what: Airline pilot monitors engine operation and functioning of aircraft systems during flights
Airline pilot checks fuel consumption against the flight plan at waypoints
Airline pilot writes fuel and times on the paper flight plan today; after the change checks the values aircraft data fill in at each waypoint
Airline pilot discusses abnormal trends with the other pilot

tasks.design: An electronic flight plan on the flight-deck tablet ({OPS_SYSTEM}) records times and fuel at each waypoint from aircraft data and shows the difference from the plan, so pilots check flagged differences instead of writing every value. Monitoring engines and systems and discussing trends stay with the pilots.
tasks.previous_blocker: Fuel and times were written on a paper flight plan at each waypoint.
tasks.enabler_now: Electronic flight plans record waypoint data on flight-deck tablets.
tasks.still_hard: A slow fuel leak shows as a small difference that needs judgement.
tasks.human_edge: Noticing that fuel burn and engine readings together point to a leak.

reach.learn: Whether fuel deviations reach dispatch sooner.

evidence.claim: Lido Flight 4D plans routes, profiles and fuel against weather and airspace restrictions.
EASA found that accuracy tests of type B tablet applications for performance and mass and balance were not always adequate.

assumptions: Boundary: from the flight in progress to the trend decision; post-flight analysis is outside.
Input contract: flight plan from dispatch; aircraft data by connection to the tablet; fallback is the paper plan.
Monitoring and discussing do not change.
The authority approves the electronic flight plan.

Priced here: aircraft data fill times and fuel at each waypoint, so s3 keeps 30 for checking flagged differences and writing values the connection misses. The journey log is a separate record, cut in sibling task 10578.

incremental.description: Airline pilot enters values by hand when the data link fails.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: older aircraft without a data connection, so fuel and times are still written by hand (7.5); high: connected aircraft as designed (18.0).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Monitor gauges, warnings and control panels, set engine thrust, calculate take-off performance and thrust settings, and cross-check them with the other pilot.

steps.what: Airline pilot monitors gauges, warning devices and control panels to verify aircraft performance
Airline pilot calculates take-off performance and thrust settings from tables
Airline pilot cross-checks the performance figures with the other pilot
Airline pilot regulates engine speed and thrust

tasks.design: A performance application on the flight-deck tablet ({OPS_SYSTEM}) computes take-off speeds and thrust settings from the flight manual data, the load sheet and airport conditions, after accuracy tests across the operating range. Both pilots compute independently and cross-check. Monitoring gauges and setting thrust stay with the pilots.
tasks.previous_blocker: Take-off performance was read from paper tables.
tasks.enabler_now: Tablet performance applications compute from flight manual data.
tasks.still_hard: A wrong weight typed into the application gives a wrong answer.
tasks.human_edge: Feeling that the aircraft is not accelerating as it should.

reach.learn: Whether load sheet data flow into the performance application.

evidence.claim: With NetLine/Load CockpitMobile, pilots run weight and balance and approve the load sheet on a mobile device.
A UK investigation found that a passenger title mapping error gave a wrong take-off weight on the load sheet.
Type B tablet applications for performance need accuracy tests against the flight manual across the operating range.

assumptions: Boundary: from the load sheet to thrust set; flight planning is outside.
Input contract: load sheet from load control; flight manual data from the manufacturer; fallback is paper tables.
Monitoring, setting thrust and cross-checking do not change.
The application passed the operator's accuracy tests.

incremental.description: Airline pilot checks the inputs typed into the application.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: load sheets change late and inputs are typed and checked again, so s3 keeps 50 (7.0); high: the application computes from the final load sheet and s3 keeps 30 (10.0).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The airline pilot keeps handling emergencies, talking with air traffic control, monitoring systems and setting thrust; paper logs, handwritten clearances and table look-ups shrink.
role.ambitious_version: A pilot with more attention for flying and the crew.

job.title: Airline Pilots, Copilots, and Flight Engineers
